Mycophenolate mofetil is now preferred to azathioprine,2,6-9 as it decreases rejection rates, although patient and graft survival rates are comparable.6,7,9 Early withdrawal of corticosteroids appears to be safe and feasi- ble in pancreatic transplantation,6,7 without an increase in rejection rates; patients may, however, require slightly higher doses of calcineurin inhibitors, which increases the risk of nephrotoxicity.7 Although the precise role of sirolimus in pancreatic transplantation has yet to be defined, it may be used with a low-dose calcineurin inhib- itor, thus mitigating renal dysfunction,2 or as a substitute for an antimetabolite,7,9 or as the chief drug in a calcineurin inhibitor-free maintenance protocol, or for episodes of rejection.7 Sirolimus used with tacrolimus may allow for rapid withdrawal of corticosteroids.9 Episodes of rejection are treated with corticosteroids or an- tilymphocyte immunoglobulins.2,7 Conversion to tac- rolimus from ciclosporin is used, and for those patients on tacrolimus, sirolimus has been tried.2 Pancreatic transplantation facilitates normal carbohydrate metabolism and has the potential to improve patient sur- vival and reduce the incidence of diabetic nephropathy. However, there has been concern over the long-term com- plications of immunosuppression,10 and whether islet-cell autoantibodies might produce diabetes in the transplanted graft (although this is certainly not inevitable with ade- quate immunosuppression).11 The incidence of hypergly- caemia induced by immunosuppressive regimens after transplantation appears to be less in pancreatic transplants than in recipients of other organs.5 Explanations for the ab- sence of a higher diabetogenic effect of tacrolimus after pancreatic transplantation compared with other solid or- gan transplants may include a more cautious dose of tac- rolimus in diabetic patients, the use of tacrolimus with cor- ticosteroid-free protocols, and the use of pancreatic grafts from young donors who may be more resistant to a diabe- togenic effect.9 One possible alternative to complete pancreatic transplan- tation is an islet-cell graft. These have rarely been success- ful,1 with insulin independence at 1 year3 only in about 10% of cases. However, the use of carefully prepared islet cells from more than one donor and a modified immuno- suppressant protocol12 has produced greatly improved re- sults.
